title: Future time
subtitle: will, be going to, present tenses for the future, future perfect and continuous, time clauses, future in the past

theory.title: Ways of talking about the future

blocks.text: Often the same future event can be described in different ways: The shop **closes** at 3 pm tomorrow. · The shop **will close** at 3 pm tomorrow. · The shop **is closing** at 3 pm tomorrow. · The shop **is going to close** at 3 pm tomorrow.

blocks.intro: Which form you choose depends on a number of things:
items: **Function** — for example, do you want to express a request, a promise or an offer?
**How you see the future event/situation** — for example, if you see a future event as a fixed event that cannot be changed, the present simple may be appropriate.
**Level of formality** — **will** is usually more formal than **be going to**.

rows.example: It looks as if Jake **will lose** his job.
The factory **will open** in July.

rows.use: Decisions made at the moment of speaking
rows.example: I know! I'll **ask** for a pay rise tomorrow.
I'll **help** you with the advertising campaign.
I promise you you **won't lose** your job.
**Will** you **give** a presentation on the sales figures?
No, I **won't give** a presentation on the sales figures.

blocks.text: For offers and suggestions in the question form, with **I** and **we**, we use **shall**, not **will**.
blocks.note: **Shall** I help you with the advertising campaign? (offer) · **Shall** we discuss this in the morning? (suggestion)

items: For requests, we can also use **would**, **could** or **can**. **Would** and **could** are more polite than **will** and **can**: **Would/Could/Can** you give a presentation on the sales figures?
For refusals, we can also use **couldn't** or **can't**. **Couldn't** is more polite than **won't** and **can't**: No, I **couldn't/can't give** a presentation on the sales figures.
In British English, **shall** is sometimes used with **I** and **we** in place of **will**: I **shall** be in touch again soon. · I'll be in touch again soon.

rows.example: Look at that wall. It looks as if it's **going to** fall down.
I'm **going to** get my degree, then get a well-paid job.
I'm **meeting** Fiona on Friday to discuss the advertising campaign.
I'm **asking** for a pay rise tomorrow.

blocks.text: Both **be going to** and present continuous can be used for intentions. However, present continuous is **not** usually used for intentions in the distant future.
blocks.note: I'm **going to work** for a really successful company one day. (not **I'm working for a huge multinational one day.**)

rows.use: Fixed future events (e.g. timetables and schedules)
rows.example: The shop **closes** at 3 pm next Saturday.

rows.use: Future perfect simple · completed situations before a certain time
rows.example: It looks as if Jake **will have lost** his job by the end of the week.

rows.use: Future perfect simple · continuing situations up to a certain time
rows.example: This time next month, I'll **have worked** at the company for exactly 25 years.

rows.use: Future perfect continuous · continuing situations up to a certain time (emphasises duration)
rows.example: This time next month, I'll **have been working** at the company for exactly 25 years.

rows.use: Future continuous · situations in progress at a certain time in the future
rows.example: This time next week I'll **be travelling** round Russia on business.

rows.use: Future continuous · situations which will happen in the future in the normal course of events
rows.example: The company Chairperson **will be arriving** on Thursday.

rows.use: Future continuous · habits or repeated actions at a point in the future
rows.example: I think that, in the future, more and more people **will be commuting** to work by plane.

blocks.text: After many time words and phrases, such as **when**, **while**, **once**, **as soon as**, etc., we do **not** use **will** or **be going to**. We use a present tense.

rows.example: I'll give you a pay rise when you **start** working harder!
I'll give you a pay rise once you're **bringing** in three new customers a week.
I'll give you a pay rise as soon as you've **proved** you're a hard worker.
I won't give you a pay rise until you've **been working** here for three years.

theory.title: Other ways to express the future

rows.use: be (just) about to · for the (very) near future
rows.example: I'm just **about to** ask for my pay rise.

rows.use: be (just) on the point/verge of · for the (very) near future
rows.example: I'm just **on the point/verge of** asking for my pay rise.

rows.use: be due to · for formal arrangements
rows.example: I'm **due to** meet my boss at eleven o'clock.
You're **to get** those reports written before Friday!
The factory **is to open** in July.

rows.use: other modals · for certainty, possibility, etc.
rows.example: I **might** ask for a pay rise tomorrow.

blocks.text: When we look back at what was the future once, we usually make the future verb forms past. **Will** becomes **would**, **is going to** becomes **was going to**, etc. Tenses such as present simple also change, by going back one tense.

rows.example: Then: I think the factory **will open** in September. Now: I thought the factory **would open** in September.
Then: I'm in a rush because the train **leaves** at 4. Now: I was in a rush because the train **left** at 4.
